summary: Names the data types used in RADIUS attributes, which implementations had long used without formal definitions. It updates earlier RADIUS specifications to match practice, building on the types in RFC 6158.

eli5.summary: Everyone had been using words like number and text without a dictionary. This writes the dictionary so RADIUS definitions are consistent.

questions: what data types does radius define
what is the radius tlv format
subtitle: A shared, IANA-managed list of the data types that RADIUS attributes carry, written down after two decades of unwritten practice.

tldr.problem: RADIUS attributes had always carried typed data such as integers, text and addresses, but the types were named inconsistently across specifications and were not managed anywhere.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8044 names and defines 17 data types (integer, enum, time, text, string, concat, ifid, ipv4addr, ipv6addr, ipv6prefix, ipv4prefix, integer64, tlv, vsa, extended, long-extended, evs), creates an IANA Data Type registry for them, and adds a Data Type column to the RADIUS Attribute Types registry.
tldr.outcome: New RADIUS specifications MUST define attributes using these types. The document mandates no changes to existing implementations, since it records existing practice.

today: RFC 8044 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 2865, RFC 3162, RFC 4072, RFC 6158, RFC 6572 and RFC 7268.

sections.title: Why RADIUS Needed Named Data Types
sections.content:
RADIUS specifications describe each attribute by name, value and data type. IANA records the name and the number in the "RADIUS Attribute Types" registry, but the data type was never managed or recorded. RFC 8044 exists to fix that gap.

The RFC lists the problems it found. The words "Value" and "String" were used recursively and inconsistently, so a field could be defined as containing itself. RFC 2865 defined "address" for IPv4 addresses, yet RFC 3162 used "Address" for IPv6 addresses. RFC 2869 repeated the "time" definition instead of reusing it, and RFC 6572 carried IPv4 prefixes without ever naming or defining an "IPv4 prefix" type.

Implementations had already solved this on their own. They use "dictionaries" that map attribute names to type values and give each attribute a data type. The RFC says it is time for the specifications to follow that practice.
sections.eli5: Imagine a class where one kid says "address" for a house and another says "Address" for a computer. Nobody knows who means what. So the teacher writes a list of exact words.

sections.title: No Mandated Changes
sections.content:
The RFC is careful about what it does not do. It mandates no changes to any past, present or future RADIUS implementation. It documents existing practice to make writing RADIUS specifications simpler, to clarify how standards are read, and to improve communication between authors and IANA.

Implementations SHOULD use the new type names in preference to ad hoc ones, but most ad hoc types are already compatible and any difference is typically only the name. The RFC also updates RFC 6158 so that every type in the new registry counts as a "basic data type".

The RFC deliberately skips some things. It creates no types for the tagged attributes of RFC 2868, because RFC 6158 says tagged attributes should not be used. It also creates none for complex attributes such as CHAP-Password, ARAP-Features or Location-Information, which are treated as type string.
sections.eli5: The new dictionary does not make anyone rewrite their old work. It just writes down what people were already doing, so future writers use the same words.

sections.title: Naming Rules for Specifications
sections.content:
The RFC introduces context-specific names for the parts of an attribute. Attr-Data is the Value field of an attribute as defined in RFC 2865, and it MUST hold a valid data type from the RADIUS "Data Type" registry. "Value" is kept only for the contents of simple types, such as an integer. Complex types get names based on the type: a vendor-specific attribute carries a vsa, whose contents are called VSA-Data.

New specifications MUST define attributes using types from the registry, and MUST follow RFC 6929 when defining a new type. Attributes can usually be described completely by their type value, name and data type, so ASCII art is limited to new or complex data types. The RFC RECOMMENDS not using ASCII art for new attribute specifications, partly because extended attributes can be allocated from several spaces, which changes the header and the Length value after the document is accepted.

A suggested attribute definition lists Description, Type (in the dotted-number notation of RFC 6929), Length, Data Type and Value. For an enum attribute, the list of enumerated values and names MUST be given. A new data type SHOULD use the format of Section 3 and have a single, all-lowercase name; vendors are RECOMMENDED not to define vendor-specific data types.
sections.eli5: The rule is to give every box its own clear label instead of calling everything "stuff". And when you draw a picture of a new box, only do it when words are not enough.

sections.title: The Simple Data Types
sections.content:
Section 3 defines the types in order, simplest first. Fields are sent left to right, and all numbers are in network byte order. The numbers assigned to types exist only for IANA tracking and never appear in a packet.

  • integer: a 32-bit unsigned integer, four octets.
  • enum: encoded like integer, but used for enumerated sets such as Service-Type. Specifications MUST define the valid values and a unique name for each.
  • time: a 32-bit unsigned count of seconds since 00:00:00 UTC, January 1, 1970. Being unsigned, it avoids a signed overflow in the year 2038.
  • text: UTF-8 text. It is not NUL-terminated and zero-length text MUST NOT be sent; omit the attribute instead.
  • string: undistinguished octets, also without a terminator, and also never zero length.
  • integer64: a 64-bit unsigned integer, eight octets.

Both text and string attributes in the standard space are limited to 253 octets of data, and the limit is lower if the data is encapsulated inside another attribute. Where a complex structure cannot be sent as TLVs, string MUST be used, which includes data opaque to RADIUS and the contents of CHAP-Password. This is stronger than the SHOULD in RFC 6158.
sections.eli5: These are the basic building blocks: whole numbers of a fixed size, a moment in time, a piece of writing, and a pile of raw bytes. Each one has a set size or a set meaning.

sections.title: Concat, Addresses and Prefixes
sections.content:
The concat type carries more than 253 octets of data in a standard-space attribute. It is otherwise identical to string. If several attributes of this type appear in a packet, they MUST have the same type code, be in order and be consecutive. The RFC RECOMMENDS no more than 2048 octets as a rough guide. It MUST NOT be used in the short extended space, the long extended space, or inside tlv, vsa, extended, long-extended or evs.

The address types are straightforward: ifid is an 8-octet IPv6 interface identifier, ipv4addr is four octets and ipv6addr is sixteen octets.

The prefix types add a one-octet Reserved field (always zero) and a one-octet Prefix-Length. An ipv6prefix is two to eighteen octets; a Prefix-Length above 128 makes the attribute invalid, and the Prefix SHOULD NOT contain more octets than necessary. An ipv4prefix is a fixed six octets; a Prefix-Length above 32 makes the attribute invalid, and an all-zero address requires a Prefix-Length of 32.

The ipv4prefix layout differs slightly from RFC 6572: Prefix-Length grew by two bits and Reserved shrank by two bits, so both fields fall on octet boundaries. Because RFC 6572 required Reserved to be zero, the two definitions are compatible.
sections.eli5: An address is like a house number written in a fixed number of digits. A prefix is like saying "everything on this street": you give the street and how many parts of the address count.

sections.title: TLV, VSA and Extended Types
sections.content:
The remaining types are containers. A tlv is a Type-Length-Value as defined in RFC 6929: TLV-Type (one octet), TLV-Length (one octet, between 3 and 255, including the header) and TLV-Data. TLVs with a length of 2 MUST NOT be sent. TLV-Type values 254 to 255 are reserved, and 26 has no special meaning and MUST NOT be treated as a Vendor-Specific Attribute. A proxy SHOULD forward unknown TLV-Types verbatim.

A vsa holds vendor data: a four-octet Vendor-Id (the vendor's Private Enterprise Number) followed by VSA-Data. It is used only in the Attr-Data field of a Vendor-Specific Attribute and SHOULD contain a sequence of TLVs.

An extended type has a one-octet Extended-Type followed by Ext-Data, and forms a "Type.Extended-Type" space. Values 241 to 255 are reserved.

A long-extended type adds an M (More) flag and a T (Truncation) flag, plus six Reserved bits. When M is set, the attribute has a Length of 255, the next attribute MUST have the same Type and Extended-Type, and the last attribute in a packet MUST NOT have M set. Fragments cannot span packets, and the reassembled data is interpreted only after reassembly. Finally, evs extends the vendor space with a Vendor-Id, a one-octet Vendor-Type and EVS-Data; it MAY appear inside extended or long-extended only.
sections.eli5: Some boxes hold other boxes. A long note can be cut into pieces that are glued back together in order, and vendors get their own drawers for private things.

sections.title: What Implementations Must Do with Bad Data
sections.content:
An implementation that does not support a particular data type MUST treat attributes of that type as string, and it is RECOMMENDED that it also treat them as "invalid attributes" as defined in RFC 6929.

When the contents do not match the type's definition, the enclosing attribute MUST be treated as invalid. Examples are values outside the allowed range for a type, text that does not match its required format, and lengths that are too short or too long.

Reserved fields are handled more loosely. Implementations SHOULD be able to receive and process attributes with non-zero Reserved fields, but MUST set Reserved fields to zero when creating attributes. This leaves room for future specifications to give those bits a meaning.
sections.eli5: If a box looks wrong or does not match its label, you set it aside instead of guessing what is inside. But when you pack a box, you leave the spare spaces empty.

sections.title: The New IANA Registry and Security
sections.content:
IANA has created a "Data Type" registry under "RADIUS Types", with registration by Standards Action. It has columns for Value, Description and Reference, and the Value and Description have no on-the-wire meaning. The initial contents number the 17 types from integer (1) to evs (17).

The "RADIUS Attribute Types" registry gains a new "Data Type" column between Description and Reference. From now on every allocation request in that registry must include a Data Type taken from the new registry.

For security, the RFC says the document concerns only registries and has no security considerations of its own. It argues that inconsistent names and poorly defined entities can lead to security and interoperability problems, and that one canonical source for type definitions makes implementations simpler and more likely to be correct.
sections.eli5: There is now an official list at a central office, and every new RADIUS part must say which kind it is. Fewer mix-ups means fewer mistakes.

fields.name: TLV-Data
fields.desc: One or more octets of attribute data.
